content.title: About
content.content: Cheese and queso are dairy products made from coagulated milk. Cheese can be hard, semi‑hard or soft, while queso (the Mexican melted cheese) usually has a softer texture and a mild flavor. Both are rich in protein, calcium and fatty acids and are widely used in cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese has been known to humans for over 7,000 years; the earliest evidence comes from ancient Mesopotamia.
Queso means “cheese” in Spanish, but in culinary contexts it often refers to a processed meltable cheese used in tacos, nachos and sauces.
There are more than 1,800 varieties of cheese, differing by aging process, type of milk and region of production.
Traditional Mexican queso is often made from a blend of melted cheese, cream and spices, giving it a characteristic stretchy quality.
Cheese rinds can be repurposed to make broths and sauces, adding depth of flavor.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese and queso provide high levels of calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Milk protein in cheese supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheeses contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Some aged cheeses contain live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: Certain cheeses contain conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), which may help maintain a healthy weight.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming cheese, especially soft and fresh varieties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses, particularly aged ones, are high in salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can cause severe reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese and queso are energy‑dense foods; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Choking hazard with hard cheese
items.content: Hard cheese chunks can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese can be enjoyed sliced, grated into salads, melted in hot dishes, casseroles and sauces. Queso is commonly used in Mexican cuisine: nachos, tacos, fajitas, and as a meltable sauce that creates a stretchy texture. To reduce fat intake, choose low‑fat cheese varieties or limit the amount of queso in recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Hard cheeses can last several months, soft cheeses up to a week. Keep queso in a sealed package to prevent drying. Discard any cheese that develops unwanted mold (except for intentionally rind‑aged varieties).

content.title: About
content.content: Ricotta is a soft Italian cheese made from the whey left over after producing other cheeses (such as mozzarella). It has a delicate creamy flavor, slightly sweet, and a smooth texture. Ricotta is commonly used in desserts, pastas, lasagna, and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “ricotta” comes from the Italian “ricotta,” meaning “re‑cooked.”
Traditionally ricotta is made from cow, sheep, or goat whey.
In Italy ricotta is often served with honey and nuts as a dessert.
Ricotta is high in protein but relatively low in fat compared with many other cheeses.
There is a “dry ricotta” variety that is further dehydrated for a firmer consistency.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ricotta provides about 11 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium in ricotta helps strengthen bones and teeth.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Compared with many hard cheeses, ricotta contains moderate salt levels, which is beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ricotta supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its soft texture and partial fermentation make ricotta gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey proteins may react to ricotta.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Ricotta contains lactose, so those with lactose intolerance should limit intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although less fatty than many cheeses, ricotta is still calorie‑dense and should be consumed in moderation for weight management.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Fresh ricotta spoils quickly; it must be refrigerated and used within its indicated shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ricotta can be enjoyed on its own, mixed with honey, fruit, or nuts. It is a classic filling for pasta, lasagna, cannelloni, and desserts such as tiramisu and cheesecakes. Add it to smoothies for a creamy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ricotta in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. It typically keeps 5‑7 days after opening. Discard if it develops a sour smell or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Apple cobbler is a classic American dessert made of baked apples topped with a biscuit‑like dough that forms a golden, crumbly crust. The apples become soft and fragrant, while the topping turns crisp and buttery.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cobbler originated in the 19th‑century United States, inspired by British pies.
Tart apple varieties such as Granny Smith are traditionally used to keep a slight acidity.
The topping is usually leavened with baking powder or simply relies on the lightness of flour and butter, not yeast.
Variations include adding berries (blueberries, raspberries) or dried fruits.
Cobbler is often served warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Apples provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Apples supply vitamin C, which aids the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The cobbler topping is typically made with a modest amount of butter, keeping the dessert relatively low‑fat.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Apple skins contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: Baked apples have a lower glycemic impact than many other sweet desserts.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Cobbler is often sweetened, so people monitoring blood sugar should watch portion size.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The topping contains wheat flour, which can be problematic for those with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While not overly fatty, a serving can be calorie‑dense due to sugar and butter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cobbler warm, typically with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, or yogurt. It can be eaten straight from the baking dish or plated individually.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or oven before serving to restore the crisp topping.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottage cheese is a fresh cheese curd product obtained by curdling milk and draining the whey. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor and a creamy, lumpy texture. Cottage cheese is eaten on its own, used in cooking, baking, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is one of the oldest dairy foods, with evidence of its consumption in ancient Egypt.
It is known by different names worldwide: "cottage cheese" in the US, "tvorog" in Russia, and "fromage blanc" in France.
Cottage cheese comes in various fat levels, from non‑fat to about 9‑10 % milk fat.
There are "small curd" (soft) and "large curd" (firm) varieties, differing by the size of the curd grains.
It is often used as a base for cheese fillings, dumplings, and classic cottage cheese pancakes (syrniki).

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cottage cheese provides high‑quality dairy protein that supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium in cottage cheese helps maintain strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Its low sugar content makes it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Live cultures in some cottage cheese varieties may support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming cottage cheese, especially low‑fat versions with higher lactose content.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey proteins can cause reactions to cottage cheese.

items.title: Added sodium in some products
items.content: Certain pre‑packaged cottage cheese varieties contain added salt, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cottage cheese can be enjoyed as a snack, mixed into smoothies, oatmeal, salads, used as a filling for pancakes, dumplings, or baked into casseroles and cheese pancakes. Sweet versions are often combined with fruit, honey, or jam.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cottage cheese in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container. It typically remains fresh for 5‑7 days after opening. Discard if it develops a sour odor, mold, or an off‑texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon-butter sauce is a classic sauce made from butter, fresh lemon juice, grated zest, salt, and sometimes herbs. It offers a bright, refreshing flavor with a balance of acidity and richness, perfect for fish, seafood, chicken, and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce originated in French cuisine in the 19th century as a variation of classic beurre blanc with added lemon.
Lemon juice not only adds flavor but also stabilizes the emulsion, preventing the butter from separating.
Traditionally the sauce is cooked over low heat while whisking constantly to keep the butter from curdling.
Finely chopped parsley or dill can be added for extra aroma.
Lemon‑butter sauce is often served in small ramekins to keep it warm.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Lemon juice is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and provides antioxidant benefits.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Butter contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: The acidity of lemon stimulates bile production, aiding the digestion of fats.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The sauce contains virtually no carbohydrates, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter provides vitamins A, D, E, and K, essential for various bodily functions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Butter is calorie‑dense; excessive consumption may lead to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from butter.

items.title: Acidic irritation
items.content: Lemon acidity can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Allergy to citrus
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to citrus fruits, causing skin reactions or swelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sauce warm, drizzling it over baked fish, seafood, chicken breasts, or vegetables. It also works as a dip for breadsticks or can be tossed with pasta for a light buttery‑lemon flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Gently reheat over low heat while stirring before serving to re‑emulsify.

mozzarella-sticks-breaded-baked-or-fried.title: Mozzarella sticks, breaded, baked or fried

content.title: About
content.content: Mozzarella sticks are cheese sticks coated in seasoned breadcrumbs and cooked either in the oven or deep‑fried. They feature a golden, crunchy crust and a warm, stretchy mozzarella core.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mozzarella sticks are a staple appetizer in many American fast‑food restaurants.
They are traditionally made from whole mozzarella blocks cut into 1–2 cm thick strips.
The breading often includes a mix of breadcrumbs, spices, and sometimes grated Parmesan.
Baked versions are lower in calories but still retain the characteristic crunch.
In some regions they are called “mozzarella sticks” or “mozzarella croquettes.”

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Mozzarella provides a good amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The cheese supplies complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Mozzarella contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Certain mozzarella varieties contain live cultures that may benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, mozzarella sticks contain virtually no sugar.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy or lactose may experience reactions.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Fried sticks are rich in saturated fat and calories, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: The breading is often salty; those monitoring sodium intake should choose a low‑salt version.

items.title: Trans fats in processed versions
items.content: Some commercial products may contain trans fats, which are detrimental to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve mozzarella sticks hot with dipping sauces such as marinara, cheese sauce, ranch, or honey‑mustard. They are convenient as a finger food appetizer or can be added to salads and pasta dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked sticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen sticks last up to 2 months; reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw oats are whole oat grains (Avena sativa) harvested and sold without any heat treatment. They have a mild nutty flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a firm texture. Oats are commonly used after soaking, cooking, or baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats belong to the grass family and are one of the oldest cultivated grains.
Raw oat kernels are called "groats" and become oatmeal only after processing.
Oats contain beta‑glucans – soluble fibers that help lower cholesterol.
Historically, oats were used as animal feed and in traditional medicine.
Oats grow best in temperate climates with adequate moisture.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help regulate blood sugar levels and reduce cholesterol.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function, nerve health, and blood formation.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in oats protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin aid in energy metabolism.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to oats.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Raw oats contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are naturally gluten‑free, they are often processed on the same equipment as wheat, so people with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw oats are typically soaked in water or milk for several hours, then used in smoothies, kefir, overnight oats, or as a base for oat bars. They can also be ground into flour for baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw oats in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage and vegetables is a dish that pairs juicy boiled or fried sausage with carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale, Swiss chard). It is prepared without potatoes and without a tomato‑based sauce, making it suitable for low‑starch and low‑acid diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support detoxification.
Carrots contain beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy greens are excellent sources of iron and folate.
Lean sausage provides a quick source of complete protein.
The dish can be adapted to many cuisines by changing spices and the sausage preparation method.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Sausage supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, potassium and magnesium, which benefit immunity and heart health.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Beta‑carotene and phytochemicals in broccoli help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from carrots and leafy greens promotes healthy bowel movement.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Absence of potatoes and tomato sauce makes the dish suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages can be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium varieties.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some sausages contain saturated fat, which in excess may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may be allergic or intolerant to certain types of meat.

items.title: Oxalates in leafy greens
items.content: Leafy greens can contain oxalates; those prone to kidney stones should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté sliced sausage until golden, then add carrots, broccoli and leafy greens, cooking 5‑7 minutes until vegetables are tender. Season with garlic, paprika and fresh herbs if desired. Serve hot as a main dish or with whole‑grain bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of water to keep vegetables from drying out. Do not leave sausage at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Aspartame is a low‑calorie artificial sweetener derived from the amino acids phenylalanine and aspartic acid. The powder form is convenient for precise dosing in cooking, baking, and beverages. It is about 200 times sweeter than sugar but contributes virtually no calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Aspartame was approved by the FDA in 1981 and has since become a common ingredient in diet sodas and low‑calorie foods.
Its sweetness comes from the combination of two amino acids rather than from sugar itself.
Aspartame degrades above 120 °C, so it is usually added to products after heat treatment.
In many countries (e.g., Japan) aspartame is labeled as E951.
It is safe for the general population but contraindicated for people with phenylketonuria (PKU).

items.title: Reduced calorie intake
items.content: Replacing sugar with aspartame helps lower the energy density of meals while preserving sweetness.

items.title: Supports blood glucose control
items.content: Aspartame does not raise blood sugar levels, making it suitable for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Preserves taste profile
items.content: Unlike some sweeteners, aspartame leaves no bitter aftertaste and mimics sugar closely.

items.title: Phenylketonuria
items.content: People with PKU must avoid aspartame because they cannot metabolize phenylalanine.

items.title: Thermal instability
items.content: At high temperatures aspartame breaks down, forming methanol and other compounds, so it is not recommended for high‑heat baking.

items.title: Individual sensitivity
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience headaches or allergic‑type reactions, though scientific evidence is limited.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add aspartame powder to cold or warm drinks, yogurts, desserts, and sauces after cooking is finished. Typical dosage is indicated on the package – about 1 g of powder replaces roughly 200 g of sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in a tightly sealed container to prevent moisture absorption. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated, but protect from direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked turnip is a root vegetable obtained after boiling fresh turnip (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa). Cooking makes it tender, gives it a mild sweet flavor and a pale creamy color. It is commonly served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip belongs to the Brassicaceae family and is closely related to cabbage, broccoli, and radish.
Archaeological evidence of cooked turnip dates back over 3,000 years in China.
In Russia, cooked turnip is often used in the traditional dish “herring under a fur coat”.
When boiled briefly, turnip retains most of its vitamins, especially vitamin C.
Red and white turnips differ in taste: red turnips are usually sharper, white turnips milder.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked turnip retains a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A 100 g serving of cooked turnip provides about 20 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports gut health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Provides folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may be allergic to cruciferous vegetables, including turnip.

items.title: Vitamin C loss with prolonged cooking
items.content: Vitamin C degrades with long cooking times, so it’s best to cook turnip until just tender.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Turnip contains complex carbohydrates that can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked turnip can be served as a standalone side, diced into salads, added to soups and stews, mashed, or baked with cheese. It pairs well with butter, dill, lemon juice, and garlic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turnip in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it – the flavor and nutrients remain well preserved.
